entry.title: An Entirely Plastic-Free Coffee Machine for $100 Off
entry.summary: Your coffee only touches glass and steel in SGC’s Brewer (plus other great Black Friday coffee deals).
entry.content:
The world of plastic-free drip coffee makers is small. Caraway recently came out with one that (sadly) isn’t on sale for Black Friday — but there are a couple of models from Simply Good Coffee that (happily) have good discounts right now. Strategist senior writer Michael Zhao first discovered the original model it when he was researching all the ways you could possibly brew coffee without plastic. Now there’s a second-generation version as well as a programmable version for people who don’t mind pre-grinding their beans and want to wake up to a fresh pot. Both have a completely plastic-free (and aluminum-free) brewing path, from the glass water reservoir through the stainless-steel internals and all the way to the carafe, also made from glass.

Though the Simply Good Coffee machines lack the array of color options, they look strikingly similar to the well-designed and much-beloved Technivorm Moccamaster. But Zhao says they’re actually even better at making coffee than the Technivorm thanks to their automatic bloom mode, which has a dedicated button to pre-wet the coffee grounds before brewing begins. Wider circular showerheads promote even extraction, and the metal internals and brew baskets conduct more heat away from the water than plastic parts would, so the brewing temperature ends up being a bit lower than ideal for some lighter roasts. They’re impressive and consistent, he says.

entry.title: The Emergency-Preparedness Items I’m Buying As a First-Time Homeowner
entry.summary: Including items to stay safe in a kitchen fire, power outage, storm, or evacuation.
entry.content:
My fiancé and I closed on our first home last month, and the entire experience has been super exciting yet stressful. Before we even got the keys, many of our family members and friends had told us new-homeownership horror stories and recommended items we should buy and keep on hand to avoid them. I quickly began compiling a list of these things, which included a fire extinguisher, a tall ladder for changing our smoke-detector batteries, water-leak sensors, and even a few reliable plungers. I knew a well-stocked emergency tool kit — with a wrench, screwdrivers, utility knife, duct tape, work gloves, and a headlamp — was critical. But as I heard more recommendations for items I’d never considered, I wondered what else we could be missing.

To figure out everything we’d need just in case, I spoke to disaster-prevention experts about the things homeowners (and renters) should have around for different scenarios, like basement floods and small fires. Just note that any emergency-preparedness products are rechargeable, which often means they contain lithium-ion batteries. Purchasing lithium-ion-battery-powered devices safely requires looking for items with a stamp from the Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory (NRTL) program, according to Kelly Ransdell, the director of public education at the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA). The NRTL certification was created by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) to ensure your electrical appliances, electronics, and home systems — from your electric toothbrush to your power tools and security cameras — undergo independent third-party testing to verify safety standards.

If you’re not sure where to begin, creating a go bag in case you must evacuate your home quickly is a key preparation step, according to Mina Arnao, founder of More Prepared, a provider of emergency-survival and disaster-readiness solutions based in Southern California. Along with your go bag, a stay-at-home kit is important too. It should contain things like bulk nonperishable meals and a larger water supply. Stephanie Fox, the national spokesperson for the American Red Cross, suggests compiling everything that’s already in your go bag — her checklist is below — but in a more robust version that can sustain and comfort your family for up to two weeks.

1. Water: one gallon per person per day
2. Food: nonperishable, easy-to-prepare, and accommodating of dietary restrictions or allergies
3. Flashlight with extra batteries
4. A radio, either battery-powered or hand-crank
5. First-aid kit
6. Prescription medications (seven-day supply) and medical devices
7. Multipurpose tool
8. Sanitation and personal-hygiene items
9. Copies of personal documents (medication list and pertinent medical information, proof of address, deed or lease to home, passports, birth certificates, insurance policies)
10. Cash

If you’ve made it this far and you’re still thinking about ways to prep, you are already a step ahead. As emergency-planning and home-safety expert Carrie, known as the Housewife Prepper online, told me, “The first few minutes of a burst pipe, small fire, power outage, storm, or other emergency can make a huge difference, and having the right equipment already in your home can prevent a manageable problem from becoming an expensive one.”

Updated on November 17, 2026
We’ve confirmed availability and updated our recommendations with the most current pricing information.

Smoke alarms are the key tool in fire prevention. Ransdell told me checking the expiration date on your smoke alarms is vital for new homeowners, especially if you’re living in an older house. “Depending on the brand,” she says, that “will either be ten years to the date they were manufactured or ten years from the date they were activated.” She adds that if you ignore this step, the detectors may work during your testing but not activate properly during a fire if the device has expired. Navy veteran Gabe Soltero, a director of operations at disaster-response organization Team Rubicon, also mentioned considering a plug-in alarm to detect gas leaks (like natural gas and propane) in addition to smoke and carbo- monoxide detectors.

I bought this commercial-grade First Alert fire extinguisher — the multipurpose brand mentioned in our guide to the best items to stock for any emergency — to keep under our kitchen sink in case we have a kitchen fire or any other small fire emergencies.

You’ll want to have fire blankets, which Arnao recommends to effectively smother a smaller fire (like a fire on the stovetop) and prevent it from spreading. They also don’t create any mess, unlike fire extinguishers.

Mykel Hawke, a former U.S. Army Special Forces captain and the author of several survival books, suggests owning a backup communication device, such as a family radio, to receive emergency alerts if cell-phone towers are down. In our guide to the best emergency radios, this Kaito model came recommended because it has standard AM/FM bands plus shortwave radio, which can be helpful in non-weather emergencies. “Shortwave-band signals bounce off the atmosphere and can travel long distances, so if you’re in a situation where all nearby communication is cut off — a coup, for example, or an earthquake that knocks out radio towers — you might be able to pick up a radio broadcast from another part of the world that offers updates on the situation in your area,” says contributor Jennifer Conrad. It can also be charged in multiple ways, including by solar panel, hand-crank generator, USB connection, a AA backup-battery compartment, or an AC/DC adapter.

A few friends who are also homeowners recommended water-leak sensors. Carrie told me it’s best to place these detectors around water heaters, washing machines, and toilets; under sinks; and near other vulnerable areas because they can catch small leaks quickly before irreversible water damage occurs. The Fibaro water sensor was previously recommended on our site by April Ramoni, a coordinator with Team Rubicon. It has an acoustic alarm and is compatible with Apple HomeKit technology, so your smartphone can also receive alarm notifications.

A wet/dry vacuum (or shop vacuum) — which is designed to remove water and debris — is another piece of gear you’ll want to have around for quickly dealing with water from leaks, flooding, or appliance failures. For the average homeowner, this DeWalt model should do the trick. With plenty of power and under 15 pounds, it’s easy to maneuver and compact for household storing.

Arnao listed flood-control barriers as helpful tools to temporarily block or divert water away from your home. These gel-filled Minnow bags from Garrison Flood Control are a sandbag alternative designed to absorb water and swelling in under five minutes to create a barrier at an entrance or doorway.

According to Carrie, a backup power source — such as a solar generator or a tri-fuel generator — can be super helpful for keeping essential appliances and devices, like your refrigerator and cell phone, running during an outage.

A portable charger like the rugged BioLite Charge 100 Max will make the perfect power station for phones, tablets, and laptops. “With a capacity of 25,000 mAh, the Charge 100 Max can recharge a MacBook Pro twice or an iPhone 17 Pro Max nearly five times,” says our tech writer Jordan McMahon.

We named EcoFlow’s Delta 3 Plus our best portable solar-powered generator overall because it offers a combination of reliability and ease of use. “It’s capable enough out of the box to run critical appliances, light enough for one person to carry, has a very fast recharge time, has a user-friendly app, and can charge from multiple solar panels for extended use during outages,” say our contributors Steven John and Sal Vaglica.

If you just need to power a few devices and want something easier to transport, Jackery’s portable power station can be charged using an AC power cord or 12V car adapter or attached to the brand’s compatible solar panels for continuous power. It can charge multiple devices simultaneously, including cell phones, AC units, and fridges.

Carrie recommends this portable generator that runs on gasoline, propane, or natural gas. It puts out enough power to run most of the essentials in your home and includes a built-in carbon-monoxide-detection system that will automatically shut down the generator if CO levels are too high (though you’ll always want to use a fossil-fuel generator outdoors and in an area with plenty of ventilation).

Emergency lighting, including rechargeable or solar-powered lights, are key so you’re not dependent on candles during an outage, Carrie told me. This handy set can be charged by solar panel or USB and can double as lanterns and flashlights.

You might also consider buying a headlamp or the beanie I own with a built-in LED light, which is removable and rechargeable with any standard USB charging cable. It’s also easy to click among three brightness settings and has enough spotlight range to illuminate a few feet in front of me.

When building your emergency go bag for an evacuation, Fox recommended items like drinking water, nonperishable food, a flashlight with extra batteries, a battery-powered or hand-crank radio, personal-hygiene products, and, of course, a first-aid kit. Hawke’s first-aid kit of choice is the MyFAK, which offers space for customization and versatile mounting options, from securing on a car headrest to carrying it over your shoulder. The MyFAK Pro version also comes with either a Windlass tourniquet or a RATS tourniquet (you can choose when checking out) to control emergency bleeding.

If you’re located in a more remote or secluded area, the offerings from Adventure Medical Kits are designed for those far from medical care. Our associate editor Jeremy Rellosa owns this one, which includes a wilderness first-aid book plus medical supplies like a trauma pad, bandages, gloves, antibiotic ointment, nonprescription medications, and more. Fox says you’ll also want to pack any prescription medications (at least a seven-day supply) along with your medical devices.

You’ll want a stash of N95 face masks if you live in an area prone to forest fires, but overall, they’re super useful to have stocked at home or in your go bag no matter where you live. This one from Protective Health Gear is our best N95 mask overall because of its comfortable yet secure fit.

In your go bag, “if you have pets, include leashes, carriers, food, water, bowls, litter, litter box, and photos of you with your pet in case you are separated,” Fox added. I own multiple of the Cleverpup collapsible bowls, which are lightweight and easy to store in my purse or car. I’ve been testing Brooklyn-based dog brand Just Fred’s new Subway Tote, which is easy to carry thanks to dual shoulder straps plus detachable short handles and an interior leash for security.

Hawke recommended this Adventure Medical Kits trauma-specific pack, which contains supplies to control serious bleeding. The QuikClot gauze is designed to stop bleeding within minutes, plus there’s a conforming bandage, trauma pad, and additional gauze and bandages. If you already own a general first-aid kit, this is a good addition.

A portable toilet in case your plumbing is disrupted is another one of Arnao’s suggestions. The Luggable Loo is a solid option that’s lightweight and has a cover (our contributor tested it on a 13-hour road trip without stopping to use a public restroom).

Hawke also says if you can’t cook at home or you’re going to be out of your house for an extended period, you’ll want to have multiple ways to cook food. We named the Jetboil our best backpacking stove because it offers superfast boiling powers and is designed to work in both hot and cold climates. Just note that the stove locks onto Jetboil’s proprietary insulated aluminum pot and requires isobutane as the fuel source.

For clean drinking, you’ll always want ways to treat your water, Hawke says. “Pumps are good but laborious. Gravity-fed filters are good for groups,” he says. Lifestraw’s Peak series straw has a microfilter to help reduce clogging from sand and is made from tough, ultraleakproof materials.

Hawke mentioned Roving Blue as another brand that sells water-filtration products. The lineup is powered by its proprietary EO3 electrolytic ozone technology, which the company claims produces highly oxygenated water that can destroy bacteria, viruses, and parasites without leaving behind chemical residues. The rechargeable water-purifier cap is designed to fit Nalgene bottles, purifying the water directly inside.

“There are quite a few products available to help homeowners prepare for natural disasters. One of them is very likely already in their possession: the smartphone-issued Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA),” says Soltero. “Authorities broadcast these to notify people quickly if they might be in the path of fast-moving storms, tornadoes, or flash floods, for example. But it’s important to ensure these notifications are enabled in a phone’s settings.”

• Mina Arnao, founder and chief executive officer of emergency-preparedness company More Prepared
• Carrie, emergency-planning and home-safety expert known as the Housewife Prepper
• Stephanie Fox, the national spokesperson for the American Red Cross
• Mykel Hawke, former U.S. Army Special Forces captain and author of several survival books
• Kelly Ransdell, the director of public education at the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA)
• Gabe Soltero, a Navy veteran and a director of operations at Team Rubicon

entry.title: Apple AirPods Pro 3 Are Down to Their Lowest Price Ever
entry.summary: Get best-in-class noise cancellation and sound quality for $100 off
entry.content:
While Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 can often be found for a discount on Amazon, I’ve never seen them this cheap before. They feature excellent sound quality for earbuds as well as noise cancellation that’s good enough for day-to-day use in the office or around town. I’m especially fond of the transparency mode on these earbuds. Everything sounds lifelike without being overbearing; I can still hear my tunes through the barista calling out my name at the coffee shop. They’re also the first pair to have heart-rate tracking, which is helpful if you don’t have (or forgot to wear) a smartwatch while working out. As for sound quality, the bass has plenty of oomph, while the mids and highs are vibrant and clear. At $150, it’s hard to beat earbuds this good.

entry.title: Everything You Need for a Power Outage, According to Experts
entry.summary: We talked to city officials and preppers to find everything you need to build a blackout kit.
entry.content:
When the power goes out, what you’ll need is a blackout kit (also called an emergency supply kit) containing all the things that’ll get you through an outage at home safely. Herman Schaffer, deputy commissioner for community engagement at the NYC Emergency Management Office, says that even though “a kit should be personalized to the needs of the specific individual,” there are essential items — your flashlights, headlamps, chargers, and first-aid kits — that every single person should have on hand. Because a power outage can be caused by any number of things — like a major winter snowstorm, for example — we talked to a range of experts, from city officials to apocalypse preppers, about what they would recommend stocking in a blackout kit to stay safe (and sane). For those who would prefer to handle the preparedness in one fell swoop, there are pre-stocked kits for that, too. For even more emergency-preparedness tips, check out our roundup here.

Updated on November 17, 2026
﻿We’ve updated this story by checking availability of the products listed, updating prices, and adding some new options.

Buying a premade emergency-preparedness kit is an option that can help you prepare for blackouts, as well as other emergency situations like extreme weather events and evacuations. According to former Strategist editor Maxine Builder, “These kits will help you and your family prepare for just about any disaster you might encounter, without expending too much extra effort on your end.” When Builder tested out several of these kits, she was impressed with this option from Ready America, which she calls “an excellent starter kit, especially given the price.” The lightweight backpack includes a first aid kit, water, light sticks, as well as other survival supplies. Builder did have this tip: “To make it your own, start by throwing out the bag and moving all the gear into a larger — and, ideally, more technical — backpack,” so you can add additional items that will suit the specific needs of your family.

If you’d rather stock your kit from scratch, our experts have plenty of advice. But before you start stocking your kit with supplies, Schaffer stresses that it is essential to keep your items in one centralized location so you can find everything you need — from a flashlight to backup medications — in the event of an emergency. This bin is weathertight to keep contents clean and dry. Plus, it is made of clear plastic, so you can easily see what’s inside.

Michael Clendenin, a retired spokesperson for Con Edison, recommends “stocking up on basic food supplies and water” for yourself and your pets, in the unlikely event that the outage lasts more than a few hours. The general rule of thumb, he says, is one gallon per person per day.

Jason Charles, president of the New York City Preppers Network, also likes this first aid kit from Thrive to treat minor injuries. However, he also recommends supplementing a standard first aid kit with your own medicine and personal products to suit your specific medical needs. On an additional health note, both Schaffer and Clendenin stressed that if you are a person who relies on assistance equipment that requires backup power, you should make sure you are registered with your utility company so that local authorities are aware of your needs.

Charles says a fire extinguisher “is a must-have, especially if you live in an apartment building that doesn’t have sprinklers.”

“We advise people to make sure you’ve got a portable battery for your phone,” says Clendenin, so that you can make emergency calls and have access to an additional flashlight and personal entertainment. Dale Goodwin, host of the Survivalist Prepper podcast, recommends portable chargers from Anker. The Nano is one of our favorite portable chargers for its built-in cable, making it convenient to carry without an extra cord.

Aaron Frankel, host of In the Rabbit Hole: Urban Survival Podcast, recommends stocking up on both AA and AAA batteries to power your flashlights, radios, and any other essentials that you’ll no longer be able to charge with a wall plug.

If you live with other people and want to be prepared for a longer outage, prepper Sharon Ross (who goes by Afrovivalist) recommends power stations from Goal Zero, which hoards enough power to quickly charge laptops as well as phones. It comes equipped with USB ports and regular outlets, and “you can charge it from a plug socket when your power is working fine,” says Ross.

The survivalists we spoke to cautioned that even batteries will eventually lose their power. Instead, for peace of mind, they recommended solar-panel chargers, which simply sit in a sunny place when you’re not using them and then provide hours of charging power should you need them in a crisis. They’ll work to recharge everything from cell phones, to external battery packs, to lanterns. Both Goodwin and Ross praised the solar chargers from Goal Zero in particular. “It’s fantastic,” Goodwin says, “because it comes with a solar panel, a battery bank, and a flashlight all in one.”

This solar generator from Jackery is another good option to have on hand. It’s compact and lightweight, has six output ports, and takes just two hours to charge it up to 80 percent capacity. (Actor Jay Duplass swears by it.)

This far more affordable solar-panel option — that charges your phone and works as a flashlight — came highly recommended to us by Charles.

Everyone we spoke to said that a light is, understandably, one of the most important items to stock in your kit. Charles says that when it comes to flashlights, a Maglite is “one of the most dependable lights on the market. They are sturdy, tough, and take batteries.”

While a flashlight is great for aiming your light, especially in nooks and crannies, almost all of our experts talked about the importance of keeping a headlamp nearby also. That’s because it frees up your hands in the dark, which makes essential tasks (or just reading in bed) easier to complete and prevents injuries because your hands are now free to catch you should trip or fall in the dark. (Schaffer adds that your headlamp should always be kept next to your bed so it’s easily accessible should the power go out when the sun’s also down.) Strategist senior writer Michael Zhao recommends this quick-charging headlamp from BioLite: “This extremely comfortable headlamp gains an hour of run time with just eight minutes of charging.”

Both Goodwin and Frankel keep glow sticks in their kits, which are a fun and effective way to light up your home, especially for kids (and the young at heart).

Coonradt and Hardy recommend this solar lighting system because it “is a great way to minimize the inconvenience” of a power outage “without spending a bunch of money on a generator.” Solar-generated light systems work much like solar chargers — according to Charles, “you let the panels charge in natural light during the day, then they produce good light at night.”

This affordable system includes a six-watt solar panel, three individual string lights, and three overhead lights (all with individual switches), a motion sensor, two USB device charging ports, a digital display for feedback on power availability, and a built-in FM radio and speaker. Plus, the battery holds a 20-hour charge.

Frankel also likes this rechargeable lantern that comes with a USB power hub.

A manual can opener is an often overlooked item, according to the experts we spoke to. “To many people’s surprise, when they go to enjoy their canned fruit cocktail when the power is out, they realize their electric can opener is useless. Having a manual can opener can literally save the day until power is restored,” explains Coonradt and Hardy. This one by OXO has an easy-to-turn knob and nonslip handles.

Schaffer recommends also keeping a safety whistle in your kit. “It helps you to alert people if you’re in trouble or need help, without having to strain your voice.” It also carries further, he says, adding that many people he knows take whistles with them when they leave the house. “Say you’re stuck in an elevator — you to be able to blow a whistle. It’s soothing just to have on you.”

This four-in-one emergency tool is also critical to have on hand, our experts say, in the event you need to turn off your gas valves or water meters (it can also be used to pry open doors or cabinets).

Two of our experts cited an emergency radio as an essential part of any blackout kit. Coby Coonradt and Cameron Hardy, hosts of The Casual Preppers podcast, explain that because the radio is “powered by battery, solar, or hand crank, it can be ready to use at any unexpected moment.”

And while people tend to stock up on essentials like food and water, they “often forget to include things that will make themselves more comfortable,” says Schaffer. He recommends adding in seasonally appropriate items that will help you manage different temperatures if your heat or air-conditioning goes out. For the winter, that means sleeping bags, like this expert-recommended one from The North Face.

And here’s a self-inflating pad to go under it.

Schaffer says, “If you are a person who relies heavily on your phone for entertainment, make sure you have things on hand so you can entertain people (and especially kids) appropriately.” Goodwin keeps games and playing cards stocked in his kit for this express purpose.

entry.title: 10 Emergency-Preparedness Items for Reasonable People
entry.summary: Get ready for a power blackout, not ‘Terminator 2’
entry.content:
Doomsday prepping, once the butt of jokes and the subject of junky television documentaries, has recently gone mainstream. Even if you don’t live in an area prone to natural disaster, you’ve probably at least thought about getting some kind of go bag together — especially as governments around the world have started literally instructing people to do so.

There are a few reasons why it feels like everybody is talking about prepping right now, says Sean Gold, the founder of survival website TruePrepper. AI is the main one. “Technological advances are going at a breakneck pace,” he says. “People are looking at cybersecurity, power-grid infrastructure, and supply chains for potential disruption from AI-led or assisted disturbances.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s new Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability (FORTRESS) initiative, which aims to make U.S. military bases operational off-grid, has also got people worried, says Gold. He adds that while fears around this are likely overblown — “FORTRESS is a long-overdue Band-Aid for vulnerabilities that have long existed” — the fact that governments here and abroad seem to be passing off the responsibility of disaster preparedness to their own citizens is worth taking note of. “FEMA has been financially gutted and is a shell of what it was, which wasn’t that efficient or timely to begin with,” he says. “In times when the very people who are charged with keeping you safe are telling you to ‘get prepared,’ the rational response is prepping.”

Spending time getting to know your neighbors is probably the best way to prepare for any troubles to come because when disaster strikes, we’re all in this together. But you can also invest in a few key emergency items that don’t take up too much storage space and can double as camping gear. Whether you’re preparing for the playground scene in Terminator 2 or a brief electrical blackout, here’s a survivalist starter pack. You can also check out our guide to emergency preparedness for new homeowners as well as a more comprehensive list of the best items to stock for different kinds of emergencies.

Experts have told us you should reserve at least a seven-day supply of your prescription medications, along with any medical devices you need, in case of emergency. A good first-aid kit is also essential. Thomas Coyne, the owner and lead instructor at Thomas Coyne Survival Schools, calls Adventure Medical Kits “the best on the market.”

Leatherman’s durable multi-tools are highly praised by preppers. This one, which comes recommended by survivalist Travis McGill, is especially suitable for emergencies — it even has a whistle and fire starter alongside several types of blade.

“In an extreme global situation, an entire country may be off-grid, but someone, somewhere, will be broadcasting,” says Mykel Hawke, a former U.S. Army Special Forces captain and author of several survival books. A hand-crank radio like this one will keep you in the loop when all else fails.

Carrying both is ideal because you’ll always have a backup, but survivalists recommend lighters over matches. And it’s also worth brushing up on your fire-starting skills — it’s surprisingly tricky for beginners.

Morgan Rogue of the prepper site Rogue Preparedness prefers headlamps to flashlights and portable lanterns so you can be 100 percent hands-free and there’s less chance you’ll put your torch down and lose it.

Should you need to treat your water, gravity-fed filters are good for groups, says Hawke.

This Jackery can charge up the devices of everybody in your household, and the solar panels really work — I’ve gone camping with this setup many times.

Face masks are always useful to have stocked at home or in your go bag, whether you’re worried about forest fires, pathogens, or both. This one from Protective Health Gear is our best N95 mask overall because of its comfortable yet secure fit.

There are four classes of fire extinguishers for four kinds of fires — ordinary combustibles, grease, electrical, and metal — but your best bet is a standard home model, which is versatile and inexpensive. Strategist writer Brenley Goertzen, who recently went on an emergency-preparation journey after purchasing her first home, keeps hers under the kitchen sink.

And you should keep copies of all your important documents (e.g., a medication list and pertinent medical information, proof of address, the deed or lease to your home, passports, birth certificates, and insurance policies) ready to go, ideally in a protective case like this one.
